encodingDesc.p: Two supplied OCR witnesses of George W. Mooney (1930), Indiana (INU) and Pennsylvania State (PST). INU is the base; selected clearer PST readings and all witness disagreements are recorded in the accompanying audit. Source wording, including unresolved OCR and editorial differences from Ihm, is retained. This is an OCR draft, not a proofread transcription. Chapter/section references align with Ihm (perseus-lat2). English inner-section boundaries are editorial and have been reviewed against corresponding clauses; printed chapter boundaries are retained. No translation is supplied from Rolfe or Gemini. Commentary section signs are preserved (including OCR $ for §). Domitian 13.3 is aligned by the consulatus septemdecim lemma where the sign is absent. Lemmas use mentioned linked to note type=commentary, following the Sidgwick model. Literal bibl references and explicit glosses are marked without invented reference expansions. Unconfirmed note openings and OCR reading-order issues remain in the review inventory. Introductory material, appendices and index remain available in the complete source-page archives; they are not included in these life-specific reading texts.

div.p: Of the origin of the Vitellii different authorities give different accounts, and accounts of the most conflicting kind; some saying that the family was ancient and noble, others that it was upstart, obscure, and even mean. This divergence I should be inclined to attribute to the flatterers and disparagers of the emperor Vitellius, were it not that at a considerably earlier period there were varying views with regard to the position of the family.

There is extant a treatise of Quintus Elogius addressed to Quintus Vitellius, quaestor of the Deified Augustus, which contains the statements that the Vitellii were sprung from Faunus, king of the Aborigines, and Vitellia, who in many places was worshipped as a goddess, and that they once reigned over the whole of Latium; that the remainder of this stock removed from the Sabine territory to Rome and were admitted among the patricians;

that traces of this stock survived for long in the Vitellian Way running from the Janiculum to the sea, and likewise in a colony of the same name, which in days gone by they had claimed to defend against the Aequiculi with a force from their own clan; that later, in the time of the Samnite war when troops were sent to occupy Apulia, some of the Vitellii settled down at Nuceria, and that their descendants many years afterwards returned to Rome and resumed their rank as senators.

On the other hand the generality of writers relate that the founder of the family was a freedman, while Cassius Severus and others as well say that this freedman was a cobbler, whose son, having acquired a more abundant fortune from trafficking in confiscated estates and acting as informer, begot by a common harlot, daughter of one Antiochus a baker, a son who came to be a Roman knight. But this disputed question may be left open.

In any case Publius Vitellius, whose home was at Nuceria, whether he was of ancient lineage or sprung from parents and ancestors to make him blush, was undoubtedly a Roman knight and a procurator of the property of Augustus. He left four sons who all rose to the highest position, all bearing the same name and distinguished merely by their forenames, Aulus, Quintus, Publius, and Lucius. Aulus died in his consulship, on which he had entered with Domitius, father of Nero Caesar; he was a man of great elegance generally, and especially notorious for the sumptuousness of his banquets. Quintus lost his rank at the time when it had been resolved, on the motion of Tiberius, that all such senators as were in any way unsuited should be picked out and removed.

Publius, one of the staff of Germanicus, accused Gnaeus Piso, the enemy and murderer of his chief, and secured his condemnation. After holding the high office of praetor, he was arrested among the accomplices of Sejanus, and being committed to the custody of his brother, he cut his veins with a penknife, and then, not so much repenting of his resolve to die as yielding to the entreaties of his friends, he allowed his wounds to be bound up and cured; but while he remained in the same custody he died of sickness.

Lucius, after his consulship, was made governor of Syria, and by consummate artfulness lured Artabanus, king of the Parthians, not merely to hold parley but even to pay homage to the standards of the legions. Later he held, with the emperor Claudius as colleague, two more ordinary consulships and the censorship as well. He also bore the responsibility of the empire when Claudius was away on his expedition to Britain. He was a man of great integrity and energy, but of very bad renown by reason of his passion for a freedwoman, whose spittle mixed with honey he even used as a soothing remedy for his windpipe and throat, not secretly or seldom, but daily and openly.

He also displayed a marvellous ingenuity in flattery and was the first to introduce the worship of Gaius Caesar as a god, when on his return from Syria he would not venture to approach him otherwise than with veiled head, turning himself around and then falling down before him. And to leave no artifice untried to curry favour with Claudius, who was a slave to his wives and freedmen, he asked of Messalina as a surpassing favour to allow him to remove her shoes, and when he had drawn off her right shoe, he carried it continually between his toga and his tunic, and kissed it from time to time. Likewise he worshipped the golden images of Narcissus and Pallas among his household gods. It was he also who used the famous words "May you do it often!" when he was congratulating Claudius on holding the Secular games.

He died of apoplexy on the day after his seizure, leaving two sons borne to him by Sextilia, a lady most highly esteemed and of no mean family, and having lived to see them both consuls, and consuls in the one year and for the whole year, since the younger succeeded the elder for six months. On his death the senate honoured him with a public funeral and with a statue on the Rostra bearing the inscription: "Of unswerving loyalty to his emperor."

The emperor Aulus Vitellius, son of this Lucius, was born on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, or, as some say, on the seventh day before the Ides of September, in the consulship of Drusus Caesar and Norbanus Flaccus. His parents were so appalled by the predictions of the astrologers who cast his horoscope, that his father always made strenuous efforts to prevent, during his lifetime, any province being assigned to his son; and his mother, when he was sent out to the legions and saluted as emperor, straightway mourned for him as one mortally stricken. His boyhood and early youth he spent at Capreae among the minions of Tiberius, and he himself was branded for ever with the by-name Spintria, and his bodily charms were supposed to have been the beginning and cause of his father's advancement.

Likewise during the following part of his life he was stained by every kind of vice and held a leading place at court, enjoying the intimacy of Gaius through his passion for driving, and of Claudius through his passion for gaming. But he found still greater acceptance with Nero, both by reason of these selfsame qualities and also by reason of a special service; for when he was presiding at the Neronean contests and Nero wished to compete among the lyre-players, but did not venture to promise to perform (though everyone kept calling for him), and accordingly had gone out of the theatre, Vitellius, purporting I to be an envoy from the insistent people, had called him back and afforded him the opportunity of yielding to their entreaties.

Thus by favour of three emperors he was advanced not only to offices of state but also to the highest priesthoods, after which he held the proconsulship of Africa and the commissionership of public works, but with varying intention and varying reputation. In the province he showed a rare integrity for two years together, for when his brother succeeded him, he stayed on still as his lieutenant; but during his office in the city he was said to have purloined some of the gifts and ornaments of the temples and to have changed others, putting tin and brass in place of gold and silver.

He had as wife Petronia, daughter of a man of consular rank, and by her a son Petronianus, who was blind of one eye. When this boy was named by his mother as her heir on condition that he was freed from his father's authority, he manumitted him, and shortly after, as was generally believed, killed him, charging him moreover with parricidal intent, and alleging that through consciousness of guilt he had drunk the poison made ready for the crime. After this he married Galeria Fundana, whose father was of praetorian rank, and by her also he had children of both sexes, but the male child had such a stammering utterance, that he was little better than dumb and tongueless.

Galba sent him to command in Lower Germany, to the great surprise of everyone. It is thought that he was helped by the backing of Titus Vinius, who at that time was most powerful, and whose good-will he had long since gained through their common support of "The Blues"; but against this is the fact that Galba had openly declared that none were less to be feared than those whose sole thought was about their food, and that even Vitellius' capacious maw could be filled with the plenty of that province, so that it is manifest to anyone that he was chosen out of contempt rather than through favour.

It is quite certain that when he was about to start he lacked provision for the journey, his domestic resources being so straitened that he had to stow away his wife and children, whom he was leaving behind at Rome, in a lodging-house garret, so as to let his house for the remainder of the year, and further he had to pawn a jewel taken from his mother's ear, to meet his expenses on the road. A crowd of creditors lay in wait for him, and tried H2 to stay his going, among them the citizens of Sinuessa and of Formiae, whose public revenues he had diverted to his own use, and he could only get rid of them by frightening them with threats of false accusation; for he had instituted proceedings against a certain freedman who was pressing him overmuch for payment, alleging that he had been kicked by him, and refused to withdraw his suit until he had wrung from him fifty thousand sesterces.

On his arrival the army, already disaffected towards the emperor and disposed to mutiny, received him gladly, with hands upraised to heaven, as though he were a gift sent by the gods, being the son of one thrice consul, in the prime of life, and of an easy, extravagant disposition. This earlier belief with regard to him Vitellius had strengthened by some fresh proofs lately given, for all along the road he warmly kissed even the common soldiers whom he met, and at every post-house and inn he was so surpassingly affable to muleteers and travellers, that in the morning he asked them one by one if they had breakfasted yet, and let them see even by belching that he had done so.

When once he had entered the camp he refused no request made by anyone, and further of his own accord he removed the degrading sentences from those in disgrace, the mourning from those whose case was undecided, and the penalty of death from those condemned. Therefore, when scarcely a month had passed, without regard to the day or hour, for it was already evening, he was suddenly haled forth by the soldiers from his bedchamber, just as he was, with only his house apparel on, and was saluted by all as emperor, and carried round through the most crowded streets, holding in his hand the unsheathed sword of the Deified Julius, which had been taken down from the shrine of Mars and presented to him by someone amid the first congratulations.

Nor did he return to headquarters until the dining-room was in a blaze through the chimney's taking fire; and when all were dismayed and troubled by what they thought an unlucky omen, "Be of good cheer," he said, "a bright light shines for us!" This was his whole speech to the soldiers. After that, when the army of the upper province also, which had earlier revolted from Galba and declared for the senate, agreed to support him, he eagerly accepted the surname of "Germanicus" offered to him by all; that of "Augustus" he postponed, while that of "Caesar" he declined for ever.

And shortly after, when news came of Galba's murder, having made arrangements for Germany he divided his forces into two, purposing to send the one part in advance against Otho, and to lead the other himself. The army which was sent in advance met with an auspicious omen, for of a sudden an eagle flew towards them on the right, and circling the standards it glided gently before them as they entered on their march. But, on the contrary, as he himself moved forward, the statues on horseback which were being erected to him in many places suddenly fell down all at once with broken legs, and the laurel wreath which he had put about his head with the most superstitious care fell off into a running stream. A little later, as he sat dispensing justice on the tribunal at Vienna, a cock perched first upon his shoulder and then upon his head. To these portents the issue aptly corresponded, for the empire which was secured for him by his lieutenants he himself was not able to keep.

He heard of the victory at Betriacum and the death of Otho while he was still in Gaul, and without delay he disbanded by a single edict every praetorian cohort, as having established a most evil precedent, and commanded them to yield up their arms to the tribunes. Moreover, he gave orders that a hundred and twenty praetorians, whose petitions he had found addressed to Otho claiming rewards for services rendered in slaying Galba, should be sought out and executed; an altogether splendid and noble act, and such as to afford good hope of an excellent prince, had he not behaved in all other matters in a way more in accordance with his natural disposition and earlier life than with the dignity of empire.

For when he had set out upon his march, he rode through the midst of cities in triumphal fashion, and sailed down the rivers in most luxurious vessels wreathed with garlands of many a kind, amid most sumptuously appointed feasts, keeping no discipline among his household or his soldiers but turning the plundering and wanton violence of all into a jest; for they, not content with the banquets everywhere provided at public expense, set free whatever slaves they chose, and paid off those who withstood them with stripes and blows, often with wounds, and at times even with death.

When he reached the plains where the battle had been fought, and some of those with him were revolted by the rotting dead, he had the hardihood to encourage them by the abominable utterance : "A slain foe smells excellently well, and still better if a fellow-citizen." However, to make the noisome stench more endurable, he drained before them a mighty measure of unmixed wine, and dealt the same to all about. With like vainglory and overbearance, as he looked upon the stone inscribed to the memory of Otho, he said that such was the Mausoleum he deserved, and he sent the dagger with which Otho had killed himself to the Colony of Agrippina, to be dedicated to Mars. On the heights of the Apennines he also held an all-night festival.

At last he entered the city to the sound of the trumpet, in a general's garb and girded with a sword, amidst standards and ensigns, with his staff in military cloaks and his troops with weapons bared.

Then more and more in disregard of every law of gods and men, he assumed the office of chief pontiff on the black day of the Allia, settled the elections for ten years, and made himself consul for life. Further, to leave no doubt in the mind of any what model he chose for the government of the commonwealth, he made funeral offerings to the shade of Nero in the middle of the Campus Martius, assembling there a throng of the state priests; and when at the ritual feast a lyre-player won his favour, he openly urged him to render something from the Master's book, and when he began the songs of Nero, Vitellius was the first to applaud, and even leaped from his seat in his delight.

After such a beginning, he directed a great part of his rule solely in accordance with the counsel and caprice of the most worthless of actors and charioteers, and especially of Asiaticus, a freedman of his own. This Asiaticus in his early youth had been debauched by vicious intercourse with him, but afterwards wearying of this had run away. When Vitellius found him again as a vendor of vinegar drinks at Puteoli, he put him in fetters, but quickly released him, and made him his favourite once more. Annoyed afresh by his excessive insolence and thievishness, he sold him to a travelling trainer of gladiators; but on an occasion, when he was kept back to appear the last at a gladiatorial show, Vitellius suddenly stole him away, and when at length he received his province he gave him his freedom. On the first day of his reign he presented him during dinner with the golden rings, though that same morning, when all the soldiers petitioned for that favour on his behalf, he had expressed in the most severe terms his abhorrence of putting so great a stain on the equestrian order.

But above all else he was addicted to high living and cruelty. He always divided his repasts into three at least, sometimes four, breakfast, lunch, dinner, and a drinking-revel, being easily able to go through them all by his habitual use of emetics. He demanded entertainment from a different host for each separate meal on the same day, and the furnishing a meal cost each host not less than four hundred thousand sesterces.

Most notorious above all others was the dinner given to him by his brother on his arrival as emperor at Rome, at which, as the story goes, there were served up two thousand of the choicest fish and seven thousand birds. And yet even this he himself outdid at the dedication of that platter which by reason of its enormous size he used to call the shield of Minerva, Warden of the City, in which he blended together the livers of scar-fish, the delicate brains of pheasants and peacocks, the tongues of flamingoes, the milky guts of lampreys, fetched by his captains and galleys as far as from Parthia and the Straits of Spain.

And being a man of an appetite not merely insatiable but also unseasonable and coarse, never, either at a sacrifice or on a journey, did he refrain, but there and then among the altars he snatched flesh and bits of spelt-cake almost from the very fire and devoured them; likewise at every eating-house by the wayside he did the same to viands smoking hot or those prepared and half-consumed the day before.

He was always ready to punish by execution anyone for any cause whatever. Men of noble birth, of his own age and schoolfellows of his, whom he had enticed to court by coaxing allurements of every kind, all but offering them a share in the empire, these he put to death in various treacherous ways, even giving poison to one of them with his own hand in a draught of cold water, which he had called for when sick of a fever.

Then he spared scarcely one of the usurers, lenders by contract, and taxgatherers who had at any time demanded payment from him either of a debt at Rome or of a toll on a journey. one of these, whom he had handed over to execution just as he was paying his respects, he immediately called back again, and when all were praising his clemency, he ordered him to be killed before his face, saying that he wished to feast his eyes. At the execution of another he had his two sons executed with him for trying to win a pardon for their father.

A Roman knight too, who cried out as he was being dragged to death, "You are And my heir," he compelled to produce the tablets of his will, and when he read that one of the testator's freedmen was named as joint-heir with himself, he ordered that both knight and freedman should have their throats slit. Some even of the common people he put to death for no reason but that they had raised their voices in abuse of "The Blues," thinking that they had dared to do this through contempt of himself and hope of a revolution.

But against no class was he more savage than against pasquinaders and astrologers; the moment one was denounced, he sentenced him to death without hearing his defence, being violently enraged because, after an edict of his ordering the astrologers to leave the city and Italy before the Kalends of October, a placard was at once posted, which ran: "The Chaldaeans also make proclamation. For the good of the State! By the said Kalends of October let Vitellius Germanicus have left the land of the living."

He also incurred suspicion in the matter of his mother's death, as though he had forbidden food to be given her in her illness, because a woman of the Chatti, in whom he reposed confidence as in an oracle, had prophesied that he would be firmly established and rule for long, but only on condition that he outlived his parent. Others relate that his mother herself, weary of the present state and fearing what was impending, obtained poison at her son's hand, and that with no great difficulty.

In the eighth month of his reign the armies of Moesia and Pannonia revolted from him; as did likewise of the armies beyond the seas those of Judaea and Syria, one of which swore allegiance to Vespasian in his absence and the other in his presence. Therefore, to retain the devotion and favour of the rest of the people, there was nothing he did not lavish both publicly and privately, observing no limit. He also held a levy in the city on such terms that he promised to those who volunteered not merely their discharge when victory was won but also all the bounties granted to veterans after their full time of service.

Later on, when his enemies were pressing him hard by land and sea, he opposed to them on the one side his brother with a fleet manned by raw recruits and a band of gladiators, on the other side the forces and leaders who had conquered at Betriacum. And after he had been everywhere either defeated or betrayed, he bargained with Flavius Sabinus, brother of Vespasian, that he should be granted his own life together with a hundred million sesterces; and straightway upon the steps of the Palace he publicly declared to the crowd of soldiers there assembled that he was retiring from the rule which he had reluctantly accepted. As all cried out against it, he postponed the matter, and when a night had passed, at dawn he came down to the Rostra in mourning garb, and with many a tear repeated the same declaration, but from writing.

When the soldiers and people interrupted him a second time, and exhorted him not to lose heart, and vied in promising him their every help, he plucked up spirit, and by a sudden assault drove Sabinus and the rest of the Flavians, who no longer feared attack, into the Capitol, where he destroyed them by setting fire to the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, while he himself watched the fighting and the fire from the house of Tiberius, where he was feasting. Not long after, repenting of what he had done and putting the blame on others, he called an assembly, where he swore and compelled the rest to swear that nothing was dearer to them than the public peace.

Next he loosened his dagger from his side and offered it first to the consul, then upon his refusal to the other magistrates, and then to the senators one after another; but when none of them would accept it, he departed as if to lay it in the temple of Concord. But when some raised a shout that he himself was Concord, he came back again, and avowed that he would not only retain the steel but would also take the surname “Concordia."

He also persuaded the senate to send deputies accompanied by the Vestal Virgins, to ask for peace or, at least, time to deliberate. On the next day, as he awaited a reply, a scout brought tidings that the enemy was approaching. Immediately therefore he shut himself into a closed carrying-chair, and with only two attendants, a baker and a cook, he made by stealth for the Aventine and his father's house, intending to escape from there to Campania. Soon after, on a slight and vague rumour that peace had been obtained, he allowed himself to be carried back to the Palace. But finding everything deserted there, and seeing even those who were with him slipping away, he girt himself about with a belt filled with gold pieces and sought refuge in the porter's lodge, fastening the dog before the door and setting against it the bed and mattress.

Already the forerunners of the advancing army had burst into the Palace, and meeting with nobody, were rummaging everything in the usual fashion. By them Vitellius was dragged from his hidingplace, and when they asked him who he was (for they did not know him), and if he knew where Vitellius was, at first he misled them by a lie. But being soon recognised, he did not cease to implore them to hold him in ward for a time, even though it were in prison, pretending that he had things to say touching the safety of Vespasian, till finally, with his hands tied behind his back and a noose about his neck, his garments all torn, he was dragged half-naked into the Forum amid the grossest insults both in word and deed offered to him along the whole length of the Sacred Way. His head was pulled back by the hair, in the manner of condemned criminals, and even his chin was kept up by a sword-point held beneath it, to force him to expose his face to the public gaze and not to lower it.

Some pelted him with ordure and with mud, while others kept shouting "Incendiary" and "Platterman," and some of the mob even twitted him with his bodily defects; for he was abnormally tall, his face was generally flushed from wine-bibbing, his belly was fat, and one thigh was somewhat crippled from having been struck on one occasion by a four-horsed chariot when he was acting as groom to Gaius while he was driving. At last upon the Steps of Groaning he was tortured lingeringly to death by the tiniest of stabs and was dragged with a hook from there to the Tiber.

He perished, together with his brother and his son, in the fifty-seventh year of his age, thus verifying the prophecy of those who from the omen which befell him at Vienna, as before related, foretold that nothing else was portended but that he should fall into the power of some man of Gaul. For he was crushed by Antonius Primus, a general of the opposing faction, who was born at Tolosa and had as a boy the surname "Beccus," which means a cock's beak.
